definition: Peripheral corneal staining at the horizontal limbus in rigid lens wearers, from drying where the lens edge stops the lids from wetting the cornea. Edge lift, diameter and blinking are modified.

The FDA regulation requiring that eyeglasses and sunglasses have impact-resistant lenses capable of passing the drop-ball test, unless the prescriber finds such lenses unsuitable and notifies the patient in writing.

source.title: eCFR :: 21 CFR 801.410 -- Use of impact-resistant lenses in eyeglasses and sunglasses.

definition: The horizontal width of the box enclosing the lens opening, in millimeters; it is the “eye size” printed on frames.

source.title: Boxing System of Eyeglass Frame Measurement | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A number describing how much a lens material disperses white light into colors. The higher the Abbe value, the less chromatic aberration the wearer notices off-center; CR-39 is about 58 and polycarbonate about 30.

A rare but sight-threatening corneal infection by a free-living amoeba, with most cases in contact lens wearers. It causes redness, light sensitivity and intense pain, and keeping lenses and cases away from water is key to prevention.

source.title: Microbial keratitis (acanthamoeba sp.) - College of Optometrists

definition: The eye’s ability to increase its focusing power for near objects, achieved when the ciliary muscle contracts and the crystalline lens becomes more curved.
Near addition: the extra plus power added to the distance prescription for reading, written as ADD in diopters.
Astigmatism in which the horizontal corneal meridian is steepest; corrected with minus cylinder near axis 090.
The goal for spherical rigid lenses: an even, minimal layer of fluorescein under the optic zone, showing the lens parallels the cornea.
The two semi-visible engravings on a progressive lens, 34 mm apart, used to re-mark and identify it. The add power is engraved below the temporal mark and the brand or logo below the nasal mark.

source.title: Lens Marking Guidelines, Version 2.0 (The Vision Council)

definition: Conjunctival inflammation triggered by allergens, with itching as the hallmark symptom along with redness and swelling.
A segmented or translating rigid bifocal that moves up on downgaze as the lower lid pushes the lens, so the eye looks through the near segment when reading.

source.title: FINE-TUNE YOUR MULTIFOCAL LENS FITTING | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: A very light, strong frame metal with little flexibility, which makes riveted designs hard to adjust.
Reduced vision in an eye that did not develop normal visual pathways in childhood, often due to strabismus or anisometropia (“lazy eye”).
The maximum amount of accommodation an eye can exert, in diopters. It declines steadily with age.
A square grid of lines with a central dot used to detect central visual field distortion or missing areas, as in macular degeneration.
Glaucoma caused by blockage of the drainage angle by the iris. Acute attacks cause a painful red eye, haloes and blurred vision and are an emergency.

source.title: Primary angle closure / primary angle closure glaucoma (PAC / PACG) - College of Optometrists

definition: A difference in the size or shape of the images seen by the two eyes, often caused by anisometropia corrected with spectacles. Contact lenses usually reduce it.
A significant difference in refractive error between the two eyes. In spectacles it can cause unequal image sizes and vertical imbalance when reading.
The American National Standards Institute, which accredits the consensus process behind voluntary US standards such as Z80.1 and Z87.1.

The American National Standard of recommendations for prescription ophthalmic lenses, which sets dispensing tolerances for power, axis, prism, add, segment position and thickness. The current widely used edition is Z80.1-2020.

source.title: Quick Reference Guide – ANSI Z80.1-2020 (The Vision Council)

definition: The American National Standard for occupational and educational eye and face protection. Basic impact eyewear is marked Z87 and high-impact eyewear Z87+.

source.title: What does ANSI Z87.1 mean in safety glasses? - HexArmor

definition: The fluid-filled space between the cornea and the iris.
Thin layers applied to a lens that use destructive interference to cancel surface reflections. It increases light transmission and reduces glare and ghost images, especially on high-index lenses.

source.title: What is an AR (Anti-Reflective) Coating? | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A form of anisometropia in which one eye is myopic and the other hyperopic.
The thin edge of a prism, opposite the base. Images seen through a prism are displaced toward the apex.
Absence of the crystalline lens, most often after cataract surgery without an implant. It causes high hyperopia and loss of accommodation.
Central touch (dark area without fluorescein) under a rigid lens, indicating the lens is flatter than the cornea. It can distort the cornea; a steeper base curve is chosen.
Central pooling of fluorescein under a rigid lens, indicating the lens is steeper than the cornea. It can cause peripheral seal-off and bubbles; a flatter base curve is chosen.
The clear fluid filling the anterior and posterior chambers that nourishes the cornea and lens and maintains intraocular pressure.
A gray-white ring of lipid deposits around the edge of the cornea, common with aging.
A lens with a surface that gradually changes curvature from center to edge. It reduces oblique aberrations and lets the lens be flatter and thinner, especially in high plus powers.

source.title: Aspheric Lenses | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A refractive error caused by unequal curvature in different meridians, usually of the cornea, so light focuses as two lines instead of a point. It is corrected with cylinder or toric lenses.
A lens whose surface flattens differently in each principal meridian, extending the benefits of asphericity to prescriptions with cylinder.

source.title: Principles of Atoric Lens Design | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A computer-controlled instrument that objectively estimates a patient’s refractive error.
The orientation of the cylinder, written from 1 to 180 degrees; 180 is horizontal and 90 is vertical. It locates the meridian that has only the sphere power.
The vertical height of the box enclosing the lens opening, in millimeters.

source.title: Boxing System of Eyeglass Frame Measurement | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Bis in die: twice a day.

source.title: List of abbreviations used in medical prescriptions - Wikipedia

definition: The power of a lens measured from its back surface, the standard measurement on a lensmeter for distance prescriptions.
A rigid lens with a toric back surface to align with a highly toric cornea.
Conjunctival infection marked by redness and sticky or purulent discharge. Contact lens wear should stop until it resolves.
A soft lens worn to protect an injured or diseased cornea from the rubbing of the eyelids while it heals.
The radius of curvature of the back central (optic zone) surface of a contact lens, in millimeters. A smaller number is steeper.

source.title: RGP Contact Lens Fitting: Complete Guide for NCLE Exam

definition: The front curve of a spectacle lens blank, chosen by the manufacturer for the prescription range; the back curve is ground to produce the needed power.

source.title: All About Lens Surfacing | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The direction the thick edge (base) of a prism faces in front of the eye: base in (toward the nose), base out (toward the temple), base up or base down.
Contact lens parameter abbreviations: base curve, overall diameter and center thickness.

source.title: GP Lens Fitting Pearls (GP Lens Institute)

definition: A quaternary ammonium preservative used in many eye drops and rigid lens solutions.
A titanium alloy (with vanadium and aluminum) that is nickel-free and more flexible than pure titanium.
Prism base directions on a prescription: base in, base out, base up and base down.
A lens with two powers: distance in the main lens and a near add in a segment, separated by a visible line.
The use of both eyes together to form a single fused image, which provides depth perception (stereopsis).
A community of microbes embedded in a protective layer that sticks to surfaces such as lens cases, making them harder to disinfect.
A rigid lens with toric front and back surfaces, used for high corneal astigmatism (commonly about 2.00–2.50 D or more) to improve alignment and correct remaining cylinder.
Chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins, with crusting, redness and irritation; it can destabilize the tear film and complicate contact lens wear.
Involuntary, sustained contraction of the eyelid muscles causing excessive blinking or closure.
The rapid closing and opening of the eyelids that spreads the tear film over the eye; incomplete or infrequent blinking contributes to dryness and staining in contact lens wearers.
A tough, acellular layer just under the corneal epithelium. It does not regenerate, so injuries reaching it can scar.
The standard method of measuring frames and lens shapes by enclosing each lens opening in the smallest rectangle (box) that touches its edges.

source.title: Boxing System of Eyeglass Frame Measurement | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The angle of incidence at which reflected light is completely polarized. Reflected glare near this angle is what polarized sunglasses block.
A handheld magnifier with ultraviolet (black) light used to view fluorescein patterns of rigid lenses.

source.title: Contact Lens Primer | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: Under the Contact Lens Rule, an hour between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Monday through Friday, excluding federal holidays, in the prescriber’s time zone; known regular Saturday hours may also count.

source.title: The Contact Lens Rule: A Guide for Prescribers and Sellers | Federal Trade Commission

definition: Back vertex distance: the distance between the back of the spectacle lens and the front of the cornea.
Clockwise Add, Anti-clockwise Subtract: the same toric axis compensation as LARS, described by the direction of lens rotation as seen by the examiner.
The California agency that registers and regulates opticians (SLDs, CLDs, RDOs and NOLDs) through its Dispensing Optician Program.

source.title: ABO-NCLE - California State Board of Optometry

definition: The corner of the eye where the upper and lower eyelids meet; there is an inner (medial) and outer (lateral) canthus.
Producing lenses in molds, the method used for most mass-produced disposable soft lenses.
A clouding of the crystalline lens that causes blurred or hazy vision and glare; it is treated by removing the lens and usually implanting an intraocular lens.
Cum correctione (with correction) and sine correctione (without correction), used when recording visual acuity.

source.title: Ophthalmic Abbreviations: Complete COA Exam Reference Guide

definition: An injection-molded plastic frame material that is light, strong and flexible. Too much heat bubbles it, and acetone or alcohol should not be used on it.
The thickness of a contact lens at its geometric center; it affects oxygen transmissibility, flexure and handling.

source.title: GP Lens Fitting Pearls (GP Lens Institute)

definition: A simultaneous vision multifocal with the near power in the center of the optic zone; common in soft multifocals.

source.title: Bifocal and Multifocal Contact Lenses for Presbyopia and Myopia Control - PMC Lock

definition: How well a lens is centered on the cornea. A soft lens should cover the cornea in all gazes, and decentration can expose the limbus or cause discomfort.

source.title: Soft Contact Lens Fit Assessment: Movement, Push-Up Test, and Centration

definition: Acuity notations for very poor vision: count fingers, hand motion, light perception and no light perception.

source.title: Ophthalmic Abbreviations: Complete COA Exam Reference Guide

definition: A painless lump in the eyelid from a blocked meibomian gland.
An antiseptic used as a preservative and disinfectant in some rigid lens care products.
The vascular layer between the retina and sclera that supplies blood to the outer retina; part of the uvea.
A lens error in which different wavelengths focus at different points, causing color fringes, especially when looking through the periphery of high-power or low-Abbe lenses.
The ring of tissue behind the iris that contains the ciliary muscle, which controls accommodation, and the ciliary processes, which produce aqueous humor.
FDA device classification under which daily-wear soft lenses are Class II; soft lenses for extended wear are Class III and require premarket approval.
A blue filter on the slit lamp or Burton lamp used to excite fluorescein dye so tear patterns and staining glow green-yellow.

source.title: Contact Lens Primer | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: An off-axis lens aberration in which a point object images as a comet-shaped blur.
A lens power that has been recalculated so the finished lens gives the prescribed effect at a different vertex distance, tilt or wrap than the refraction assumed.

source.title: Vertex Distance, Effective Power and Compensated Power (National Academy of Opticianry)

definition: Retinal photoreceptors responsible for color and fine detail in bright light; concentrated in the fovea.
The requirement that prescribers ask patients to sign a statement confirming they received their contact lens prescription and keep the confirmation for at least three years.

source.title: The Contact Lens Rule: A Guide for Prescribers and Sellers | Federal Trade Commission

definition: A small, round beam directed through the anterior chamber in a dark room to look for floating cells and flare.
The thin, transparent mucous membrane lining the inside of the eyelids (palpebral) and covering the white of the eye (bulbar).
Inflammation of the conjunctiva (“pink eye”), which may be bacterial, viral or allergic.

A thin lens worn directly on the tear film over the cornea to correct vision or for cosmetic or therapeutic reasons. In the US every contact lens, including plano cosmetic lenses, is a prescription medical device.
California’s individual registration (CLD) to fit and adjust contact lenses without direct supervision. Applicants must pass the NCLE exam.

source.title: ABO-NCLE - California State Board of Optometry

definition: A small, round, sterile peripheral corneal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect and an intact Bowman’s layer, more common with extended wear. It usually resolves when lens wear stops.

source.title: Contact Lens-related Complications: A Review (J Ophthalmic Vis Res, PMC)

definition: Under federal rule, a contact lens prescription must be valid for at least one year unless a documented medical reason justifies a shorter period; state law may set a longer minimum.

source.title: FAQs: Complying with the Contact Lens Rule | Federal Trade Commission

definition: The FTC rule (16 CFR Part 315) implementing the FCLCA. Prescribers must release the contact lens prescription automatically after the fitting, and sellers may sell only on a prescription they have received or verified.

source.title: eCFR :: 16 CFR Part 315 -- Contact Lens Rule

definition: An acute inflammatory reaction of the cornea and conjunctiva linked to overnight lens wear, with sudden one-sided pain, light sensitivity, tearing, limbal redness and small corneal infiltrates. Endotoxins from Gram-negative bacteria on the lens are a commonly cited cause.
Difficulty turning the eyes inward for near work, causing eyestrain, headaches or double vision when reading.
The clear, dome-shaped front surface of the eye and its most powerful refracting surface, about two-thirds of the eye’s focusing power. It is avascular and gets oxygen mainly from the air and tears.
A scratch or loss of corneal epithelium that is painful and stains with fluorescein.
Swelling of the cornea from excess fluid, which causes haze and reduced vision; in lens wearers it usually reflects hypoxia.
A single layer of cells lining the back of the cornea that pumps fluid out of the stroma to keep it clear. The cells do not regenerate.
The outermost layer of the cornea, a few cells thick, which regenerates quickly after minor injury and is the layer that stains with fluorescein when damaged.
Oxygen deprivation of the cornea from lenses with too little oxygen transmissibility (Dk/t), causing corneal swelling, especially with overnight wear.

source.title: SILICONE HYDROGELS: FOUR DECADES OF NEW CHEMISTRY IN CONTACT LENSES | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: Growth of new blood vessels into the normally clear cornea, often from chronic hypoxia with contact lens wear. Management includes higher-Dk lenses, reduced wear time or discontinuing wear.
The thick middle layer of the cornea, made of about 200 stacked layers (lamellae) of regularly arranged collagen fibrils.
An instrument that maps the curvature of most of the corneal surface, usually by analyzing reflected concentric (Placido) rings. It detects irregular astigmatism and keratoconus.

A lens-induced change in corneal shape from GP or thick, stiff soft lenses (for example an overly steep or decentered lens), causing irregular astigmatism, distorted mires and spectacle blur. Treatment is a break from lens wear and a refit.
The narrow channel of a progressive lens through which power increases from distance to near. Corridor length affects the minimum fitting height the frame needs.

source.title: What Is A Progressive Lens? | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: An objective test in which each eye is covered and uncovered while the patient fixates, revealing tropias and phorias by the movement of the eyes.
Allyl diglycol carbonate, the standard “hard resin” plastic lens material (index 1.498, Abbe 58). It is about half the weight of glass, dyes easily and has low chromatic aberration.
The angle of incidence, measured inside the denser medium, beyond which light is totally internally reflected instead of refracting out.
The traditional ophthalmic glass (index 1.52, Abbe about 59). It is scratch resistant with excellent optics but heavy, and it must be tempered to be impact resistant.

source.title: How to Choose Lens Material | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The clear, flexible lens behind the iris that changes shape to focus at different distances. It hardens with age (presbyopia) and can cloud (cataract).
An aberration in which a flat object is imaged on a curved surface, so the edges and center of the image are not in focus at the same time.
The prescription component that corrects astigmatism by adding power in only one meridian. It can be written in plus- or minus-cylinder form.
A lens with power in only one meridian; its axis meridian has no power. Combined with a sphere it corrects astigmatism.
A surfactant cleaner rubbed on the lens to remove debris and deposits before disinfection, commonly used with rigid lenses.
A wearing schedule in which lenses are removed before sleep every night.
In the older datum system, the horizontal line halfway between horizontal tangents at the top and bottom of the lens; the boxing system replaced it.

source.title: Boxing System of Eyeglass Frame Measurement | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Distance between lenses: the shortest distance between the nasal edges of the two boxed lens openings, often called the bridge size.

source.title: Boxing System of Eyeglass Frame Measurement | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Moving a lens’s optical center away from the geometric center of the frame’s lens opening, usually to match the wearer’s PD or to create prescribed prism.

source.title: Prism by Decentration | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A plano lens that changes the appearance of the eye. It still requires a valid prescription and proper fitting.
A localized area of corneal thinning from drying next to an elevated lesion or a lens edge.
Protein, lipid or other tear components that build up on lens surfaces, reducing comfort, vision and wettability. Ionic, high-water lenses attract more protein.

source.title: Soft Contact Lens Materials: HEMA, Silicone Hydrogel, and FDA Groups

definition: The thin basement membrane between the corneal stroma and the endothelium.
Damage to the retinal blood vessels caused by diabetes, a leading cause of vision loss in working-age adults.
A slit lamp technique using a broad, diffused beam at an angle for a low-magnification overview of the lids, conjunctiva, cornea and lens fit.

source.title: How to Use a Slit Lamp - American Academy of Ophthalmology

definition: Small indentations in the corneal epithelium caused by bubbles trapped under a rigid lens with excessive clearance.
The unit of lens power, equal to the reciprocal of the focal length in meters (D = 1/f). A 2.00 D lens focuses parallel light at 50 cm.
Double vision; binocular diplopia from misaligned eyes can be relieved with prism.
Slit lamp illumination in which the beam and microscope are focused on the same spot; it includes the parallelepiped and optic section.
The variation of a material’s refractive index with wavelength, which spreads white light into its component colors. Dispersion is what the Abbe value measures.
As the FDA defines it, a lens used once and discarded; a true daily disposable is replaced with a new pair every day.
The manufacturer-specified point, often inside a circle mark on a progressive, where the distance sphere, cylinder and axis are verified.

source.title: Lens Marking Guidelines, Version 2.0 (The Vision Council)

definition: A caliper-like instrument that measures vertex distance from the closed eyelid to the back surface of the lens.
An aberration in which magnification changes from the center to the edge of the field. Plus lenses produce pincushion distortion and minus lenses produce barrel distortion.
Dk is a material’s oxygen permeability; Dk/t is oxygen transmissibility, the Dk divided by the lens thickness t.

source.title: SILICONE HYDROGELS: FOUR DECADES OF NEW CHEMISTRY IN CONTACT LENSES | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: The FDA referee test for dress eyewear: a 5/8-inch steel ball weighing about 0.56 oz is dropped 50 inches onto the lens, which must not fracture.

source.title: eCFR :: 21 CFR 801.410 -- Use of impact-resistant lenses in eyeglasses and sunglasses.

definition: A disorder of the tear film from too little tear production or too much evaporation, causing irritation, fluctuating vision and contact lens intolerance.
A red-green test used to refine the sphere: letters clearer on red suggest more minus is needed, clearer on green suggest more plus (or less minus).
Distance vision: the part of a prescription for far viewing.
Outward turning of the eyelid margin, usually the lower lid, exposing the inner lid surface.
The distance the edge of a rigid lens stands off the cornea, created by its peripheral curves. Too little causes seal-off; too much causes discomfort and decentration.

source.title: RGP Contact Lens Fitting: Complete Guide for NCLE Exam

definition: A polished finish on the edge of a lens, often used on rimless and semi-rimless eyewear for appearance, though some wearers notice rainbows or internal reflections from polished edges.

source.title: Polished Lens Edges, Friend or Foe?

definition: Cutting an uncut lens to the shape and size of the frame’s lens opening with the optical center or fitting cross positioned correctly, then finishing the edge.

source.title: What is Lens Edging/Finishing? | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Twice the longest radius from the boxing (geometric) center to the edge of the lens shape. It is used with decentration to find the minimum blank size.

source.title: How to Calculate Effective Diameter: Complete ABO Exam Guide | Opterio

definition: The power a lens actually delivers to the eye at a given position. Moving a plus lens away from the eye increases its effective power; moving a minus lens away decreases it.

source.title: Vertex Distance, Effective Power and Compensated Power (National Academy of Opticianry)

definition: The full range of electromagnetic radiation by wavelength, from gamma rays and X-rays through ultraviolet, visible light and infrared to radio waves.

source.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Vision | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The refractive state in which parallel light focuses on the retina with accommodation relaxed, so no correction is needed for distance.
Variation in the size of corneal endothelial cells, associated with long-term hypoxic contact lens wear.

source.title: Managing Contact Lens Complications | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: Inward turning of the eyelid margin so the lashes rub against the eye.
A cleaner, usually a tablet, that removes protein deposits from lenses on a weekly basis when daily cleaning is not enough.
Excess tearing that overflows onto the cheek.
Mild, usually self-limited inflammation of the tissue between the conjunctiva and sclera.
Tiny intraepithelial inclusions seen with retroillumination, a sign of chronic corneal hypoxia, especially with extended wear of low-Dk lenses.

source.title: Managing Contact Lens Complications | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: A latent tendency of the eyes to turn inward when fusion is broken.
A manifest inward turning of one eye.
A bifocal whose segment line runs across the full width of the lens, giving the widest near field. The segment optical center is on the line, so there is no image jump.

source.title: Bifocal Types & Segment Styles: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: A latent tendency of the eyes to turn outward when fusion is broken.
A manifest outward turning of one eye.
Approved overnight wear, from one to six nights or up to 30 days of continuous wear depending on the lens; the eyes should then rest without lenses for at least one night.
The six muscles that move each eye: the medial, lateral, superior and inferior recti and the superior and inferior obliques.

source.title: Extraocular Muscles | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The FTC rule (16 CFR Part 456) requiring ophthalmologists and optometrists to give patients a copy of their eyeglass prescription immediately after a refractive exam, whether or not they ask and before offering to sell glasses, at no extra charge.

source.title: eCFR :: 16 CFR Part 456 -- Ophthalmic Practice Rules (Eyeglass Rule)

definition: The movable fold of skin and muscle that protects the eye and spreads tears with each blink. Lid tension and position strongly influence contact lens fit and movement.
The horizontal curvature or wrap of the frame front so the temporal edges sit closer to the face than the nasal edges. High wrap may require compensated lens powers.

source.title: Vertex Distance, Effective Power and Compensated Power (National Academy of Opticianry)

term: Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act
definition: The federal law, signed in December 2003, giving consumers the right to their contact lens prescription and setting the seller verification system that the FTC enforces through the Contact Lens Rule.

source.title: Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act - Wikipedia

definition: The farthest point the eye can see clearly with accommodation relaxed. It is at infinity in emmetropia and in front of the eye in myopia.
The US Food and Drug Administration, which regulates contact lenses, lens care products and spectacle lenses as medical devices and enforces the impact-resistance rule.

The FDA classification of hydrogel materials by water content and ionic charge: Group I low-water nonionic, II high-water nonionic, III low-water ionic, IV high-water ionic. Silicone hydrogels form Group V.

source.title: List of soft contact lens materials - Wikipedia

definition: A tiny hole drilled through a rigid or scleral lens to improve tear exchange or release trapped bubbles.

source.title: GP Lens Fitting Pearls (GP Lens Institute)

definition: The suffix used in the adopted (USAN) names of hydrophilic soft lens materials, such as etafilcon A or balafilcon A.

source.title: List of soft contact lens materials - Wikipedia

definition: The manufacturer-specified reference mark on a progressive lens that is placed in front of the pupil, usually at pupil center, when fitting.

source.title: Lens Marking Guidelines, Version 2.0 (The Vision Council)

definition: For progressives, the vertical distance from the lowest point of the lens opening to the pupil center, where the fitting cross is placed.

source.title: Bifocal Types & Segment Styles: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: The three points where a well-fitted frame should touch the head: the nose and the top of each ear.
A D-shaped bifocal segment with a straight top line, the most popular lined bifocal. Common widths are 28 mm (FT-28) and 35 mm (FT-35), with the segment optical center about 5 mm below the line.

source.title: Bifocal Types & Segment Styles: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: Small specks or strands that drift across vision, caused by debris in the vitreous; a sudden increase with flashes needs prompt evaluation.
An orange dye that fluoresces green under cobalt blue light. It shows rigid lens fitting patterns and stains areas of corneal epithelial damage.
The distribution of fluorescein-stained tears under a rigid lens, read for the central (apical) relationship, peripheral clearance, position, movement and wetting.

source.title: Contact Lens Primer | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: The distance from a lens to the point where parallel light is brought to focus (or appears to diverge from). It is the reciprocal of lens power in diopters.
The pit at the center of the macula packed with cones; it gives the sharpest visual acuity.
The distance between the geometric centers of the two lens openings, equal to A + DBL. Also called the geometric center distance.

source.title: Boxing System of Eyeglass Frame Measurement | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A lens surfaced point by point with computer-controlled generators, allowing designs customized to the prescription and to frame and wearer measurements.
A planned replacement schedule (for example every two weeks or monthly) in which lenses are cleaned and disinfected between wears and discarded on schedule.
A thin lens made of concentric grooves that reproduce the effect of a much thicker lens. Fresnel press-on prisms and lenses are used for temporary or trial correction.
The power measured from the front surface of a lens; adds of multifocals are typically checked this way with the front of the lens against the lensmeter stop.
A rigid lens with a toric front surface and spherical back, used to correct residual astigmatism; it needs prism ballast or truncation to stay oriented.
The Federal Trade Commission, which enforces the Eyeglass Rule and the Contact Lens Rule.

source.title: Complying with the Eyeglass Rule | Federal Trade Commission

definition: A progressive loss of corneal endothelial cells that leads to corneal swelling and blurred vision, often worse in the morning.
A glass bifocal made by fusing a higher-index glass button into a depression in the main lens, creating the add.

source.title: Bifocal Types & Segment Styles: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: The center of the boxed lens opening, where the horizontal and vertical midlines of the box cross.

source.title: Boxing System of Eyeglass Frame Measurement | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A common contact lens reaction of the upper tarsal conjunctiva with enlarged papillae (over 0.3 mm), itching, mucus, reduced lens tolerance and excessive or superior lens movement.

source.title: Contact Lens-related Complications: A Review (J Ophthalmic Vis Res, PMC)

definition: A group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, often associated with raised intraocular pressure, causing progressive loss of peripheral vision.
Mucus-secreting cells in the conjunctiva that supply the mucin layer of the tear film.
A molded thermoplastic (nylon-family) frame material that is light, flexible, durable and hypoallergenic; it is glazed cold or with only slight heat.
Guttae, Latin for drops, used in eye drop instructions.

source.title: List of abbreviations used in medical prescriptions - Wikipedia

definition: Hora somni: at bedtime.

source.title: List of abbreviations used in medical prescriptions - Wikipedia

definition: A light blue or other tint in a clear lens that makes it easier to see when handling, without changing eye color.

A treatment that heats and rapidly cools a glass lens to make it impact resistant. Under 21 CFR 801.410, glass lenses must be made impact resistant and each finished glass Rx lens individually tested.

source.title: eCFR :: 21 CFR 801.410 -- Use of impact-resistant lenses in eyeglasses and sunglasses.

definition: Hydroxyethyl methacrylate, the monomer of the original soft lens material (polymacon) and the basis of many conventional hydrogels.
A corneal infection by herpes simplex virus, classically showing a branching (dendritic) ulcer that stains with fluorescein; it can recur.

source.title: Herpes simplex keratitis (HSK) - College of Optometrists

definition: A latent eye misalignment that is held in check by fusion and appears only when binocular vision is broken, as during a cover test.
Short-wavelength violet-blue visible light, roughly 400–450 nm. Some lens coatings and tints are marketed to filter it.

source.title: Biological effects of high-energy visible light - Wikipedia

definition: A lens made of a material with a higher refractive index than CR-39 (1.60 and above). It is thinner for the same power but usually has a lower Abbe value and more surface reflection, so AR coating is recommended.

source.title: How to Choose Lens Material | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, which protects the privacy and security of patients’ health information.
aliases: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act

source.title: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act - Wikipedia

definition: A screening test for strabismus in which the examiner compares the position of the corneal light reflections in the two eyes.
Benchmarks from Holden and Mertz for the oxygen transmissibility needed to avoid corneal edema; a Dk/t of about 87 is the commonly cited target for safe extended (overnight) wear.

source.title: Soft Contact Lens Materials: HEMA, Silicone Hydrogel, and FDA Groups

definition: A painful, infected gland at the lid margin, commonly called a stye.
The horizontal width of the visible iris, used to estimate corneal diameter and choose a lens diameter. A large HVID may need a larger or steeper lens and a small one a smaller or flatter lens.

source.title: In-Contact Chapter 10: Fitting Soft Contact Lenses (Contamac)

definition: A lens with a rigid gas permeable center and a soft outer skirt, aiming for rigid-lens optics with soft-lens comfort.
A water-absorbing polymer network; conventional soft lenses are hydrogels whose oxygen permeability rises with water content.
A preservative-free disinfection system using 3% hydrogen peroxide that must be neutralized to water and saline before lenses are worn; useful for patients sensitive to preservatives.

source.title: Contact Lenses: Safe Use of Hydrogen Peroxide Solution | FDA

definition: A top coat on an AR lens that repels water so droplets bead and the lens is easier to clean.

source.title: What is an AR (Anti-Reflective) Coating? | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Farsightedness: parallel light focuses behind the retina with accommodation relaxed. It is corrected with plus lenses.
A manifest upward deviation of one eye relative to the other.
Blood in the anterior chamber, usually after blunt trauma.

The sudden apparent upward shift of an object as the eye crosses a bifocal segment line, caused by base-down prism at the top of the segment. It is least with a segment whose optical center is at the segment top, such as an Executive.

source.title: Bifocal Types & Segment Styles: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: A spectacle or sunglass lens capable of passing the FDA drop-ball test. Federal rule 21 CFR 801.410 requires impact-resistant lenses unless the prescriber directs otherwise in writing.

source.title: eCFR :: 21 CFR 801.410 -- Use of impact-resistant lenses in eyeglasses and sunglasses.

definition: The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in a material (n = c/v). A higher index bends light more, so less curvature is needed for a given power and the lens can be thinner.
Viewing tissue next to, rather than in, the illuminated area, which reveals subtle, refractile or transparent lesions.
Corneal inflammation with white cell infiltrates, caused by immune responses to bacteria or toxins on the lens or lid rather than active infection.

source.title: Keratitis, CL-associated infiltrative - College of Optometrists

definition: Radiation with wavelengths longer than visible red light but shorter than microwaves.
Inward (nasal) decentration of a multifocal segment relative to the distance optical center so the near zone lines up with the converged eyes.

source.title: Quick Reference Guide – ANSI Z80.1-2020 (The Vision Council)

definition: A rigid lens fit in which the lens rides centrally between the lids without being held by the upper lid.

source.title: Contact Lens Primer | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: Intraocular lens, an artificial lens implanted in the eye, usually to replace the natural lens after cataract removal.
A lens material with a surface charge that attracts tear proteins; ionic high-water (Group IV) lenses tend to deposit the most.

source.title: Soft Contact Lens Materials: HEMA, Silicone Hydrogel, and FDA Groups

definition: Intraocular pressure, measured by tonometry in millimeters of mercury.
The colored, muscular diaphragm in front of the crystalline lens that controls pupil size and the amount of light entering the eye.
Astigmatism whose principal meridians are not perpendicular or whose curvature varies unevenly, as in keratoconus. It is best corrected with rigid lenses that replace the corneal surface optically.
A color vision test using plates of colored dots that form numbers, used to screen for red-green color deficiency.
A lens with equal plus and minus cylinder at right angles, flipped in front of the eye during refraction to refine cylinder axis and power.
The two principal corneal curvature measurements from keratometry, recorded as flat K and steep K with their meridians; the difference is the corneal astigmatism.
Inflammation of the cornea, which may be infectious (bacterial, viral, fungal, amoebic) or noninfectious.
A progressive thinning and cone-shaped bulging of the cornea causing irregular astigmatism. Rigid, hybrid and scleral lenses are mainstays of visual correction.
An instrument that measures the curvature of the central anterior cornea in its two principal meridians, giving K readings in diopters or millimeters.
The gland in the upper outer orbit that produces the aqueous portion of the tears.
Left Add, Right Subtract: if a toric lens’s orientation mark rotates to the examiner’s left, add the amount of rotation to the axis; if to the right, subtract it.
Making a lens by cutting and polishing a disk of material on a computer-controlled (CNC) lathe, used for rigid lenses and custom soft lenses.
Rinsing the case with fresh solution, air-drying it and replacing it at least every three months (preferably monthly) to prevent contamination; tap water should never be used.

source.title: Contact Lens-related Complications: A Review (J Ophthalmic Vis Res, PMC)

definition: A dial gauge with three pins that measures the surface curvature of a lens and displays it as surface power in diopters. Also called a Geneva lens measure.
How far a soft lens trails behind the cornea when the eye moves to the side or up; little or no lag suggests a tight fit.

source.title: Evaluating and Recording Soft Contact Lens Fit (J. Wolffsohn, DOCET)

definition: The distance a lens moves with each blink. About 0.25–0.50 mm is typical for a well-fitting soft lens; much less suggests a tight lens and over 1.0 mm a loose lens.

source.title: Soft Contact Lens Fit Assessment: Movement, Push-Up Test, and Centration

definition: The formula relating a lens’s power to its index and the radii of its two surfaces. For a thin lens, power is approximately the sum of front and back surface powers.
An instrument that measures the sphere, cylinder, axis, prism and add of spectacle and contact lenses and marks the optical center. Also called a lensometer or focimeter.

A high-power lens with the prescription confined to a small central aperture surrounded by a thin carrier, used to reduce weight and thickness for very high plus (aphakic) or minus (myodisc) prescriptions.

source.title: eCFR :: 21 CFR 801.410 -- Use of impact-resistant lenses in eyeglasses and sunglasses.

definition: A rigid lens fitting philosophy in which the upper lid holds the lens in a superior position and carries it with each blink.

source.title: Contact Lens Primer | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: The border zone where the cornea meets the sclera; it contains the stem cells that renew the corneal epithelium.
A vital dye that stains damaged conjunctival and corneal cells with less stinging than rose bengal, used in dry eye assessment.
Vision loss that cannot be fully corrected with ordinary glasses, contacts, medicine or surgery and interferes with daily activities.
An optical or electronic device, such as a high-add reader, magnifier or telescope, that helps people with visual impairment use their remaining vision.

source.title: Low Vision Care: An Overview | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The small central area of the retina responsible for detailed central and color vision.
Age-related deterioration of the macula that causes loss of central vision; it occurs in dry and wet forms.
A lens of parallel cylinders that turns a point of light into a line, used to measure phorias.
Blockage or abnormal secretion of the meibomian glands, a common cause of evaporative dry eye and posterior blepharitis.
Oil glands along the edges of the eyelids that secrete the lipid layer of the tear film, slowing tear evaporation.
A flexible titanium alloy (sold as Flexon) that returns to its shape after being twisted or bent; it is light, corrosion resistant and hypoallergenic.

source.title: How to Choose the Glasses Frame Material That's Right for You - American Academy of Ophthalmology

definition: A lens with one convex and one concave surface. Nearly all modern spectacle lenses are meniscus in form, with the convex side facing out.
A sight-threatening corneal infection; in lens wearers the risk rises sharply with extended (overnight) wear. The lens should be removed and the patient referred urgently.

source.title: Contact Lens-related Complications: A Review (J Ophthalmic Vis Res, PMC)

definition: The smallest uncut lens diameter that will fill a frame opening: commonly estimated as ED + total decentration + 2 mm (MBS = ED + (frame PD − patient PD) + 2).

source.title: Minimum Blank Size (MBS): Formula and Why It Matters

definition: A diverging lens, thinner in the center than at the edge, that spreads parallel light as if from a virtual focus. It corrects myopia and acts like two prisms apex to apex.
A way of writing a sphero-cylindrical prescription with the cylinder as a negative number. In the US it is the convention used by most optometrists.
A highly reflective coating on the front of sunglass lenses that hides the eyes from view and further reduces glare outdoors.

source.title: Lens Coatings & Treatments: Enhancing Vision and Function | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Combining multifocal and single-vision lenses, or two multifocals biased differently, to improve vision at all distances.
A measure of a lens material’s stiffness. Higher-modulus lenses, such as early silicone hydrogels, resist flexing and are linked to mechanical complications like SEALs and papillary conjunctivitis.

source.title: Modulus and its Effect on Contact Lens Fit | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: A copper-nickel alloy and the most widely used frame metal. It is easy to adjust and corrosion resistant, but its nickel content can cause skin reactions in some wearers.
The distance from the center of the bridge of the nose to the center of each pupil, measured separately for each eye; important for progressives and for asymmetric faces.
Fitting one eye (usually the dominant eye) for distance and the other for near with single-vision lenses.
Small, motionless spheres of debris under high-Dk silicone hydrogel lenses that indent the corneal epithelium and leave imprints that pool fluorescein; they are generally benign.

source.title: Mucin Balls and High Dk Soft Lenses | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: A single solution that cleans, rinses, disinfects and stores soft lenses. Studies show multipurpose solutions are not effective against Acanthamoeba.
Nearsightedness: parallel light focuses in front of the retina, so distance vision is blurred. It is corrected with minus lenses.
The channel that drains tears from the lacrimal sac into the nose; tears enter the system through the puncta at the inner lid margins.
The pupillary distance when the eyes converge to a reading distance, typically a few millimeters less than the distance PD; used to place bifocal segments and reading lenses.
The closest point the eye can focus on using full accommodation. It recedes with age, which is the basis of presbyopia.
The manufacturer-specified point on a multifocal or progressive lens where the add power is measured.

source.title: Lens Marking Guidelines, Version 2.0 (The Vision Council)

definition: Finding an unknown lens’s power by moving it and watching a target: against motion means plus power, with motion means minus, and adding trial lenses until motion stops reveals the power.
The step that converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, using a catalytic disc in the special case or a tablet. Putting unneutralized peroxide in the eye causes burning and corneal damage.

source.title: Contact Lenses: Safe Use of Hydrogen Peroxide Solution | FDA

definition: The approximate power of a lens found by adding its front and back surface powers, ignoring thickness.

source.title: Understanding Sphere, Cylinder, and Axis in the Eyeglass Lens Prescription | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: California’s registration (NOLD) for businesses outside California that deliver ophthalmic lenses to patients in the state.

source.title: Frequently Asked Questions – Opticians - California State Board of Optometry

definition: Adjustable pads on pad arms that rest on the sides of the nose and support most metal frames; their angles and spacing control frame height and vertex distance.
Near vision: the reading part of a prescription or the near segment of a multifocal.
A strong, lightweight frame plastic often used for sports, safety and wraparound frames because it molds easily.

source.title: How to Choose the Glasses Frame Material That's Right for You - American Academy of Ophthalmology

definition: Involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of the eyes.
An aberration that appears when light passes obliquely through a spherical lens, creating two separate line foci. Best-form (corrected curve) and aspheric lens designs minimize it for off-axis gaze.
Intraocular pressure higher than normal without optic nerve damage or field loss; it is a risk factor for glaucoma.
Oculus dexter, Latin for the right eye (the patient’s right).
A top coat that resists oils and skin smudges, making the lens surface easier to keep clean.

source.title: What is an AR (Anti-Reflective) Coating? | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A bifocal whose segment is formed from the same piece of material as the rest of the lens, as in all plastic multifocals and the Executive and Ultex styles.

source.title: Bifocal Types & Segment Styles: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: A hydrogen peroxide system that neutralizes in the same case during the soak so no rinse is needed before insertion; catalytic disc systems may give too little exposure time to kill Acanthamoeba.
A medical doctor (MD or DO) specializing in eye disease and surgery who also prescribes corrective lenses.
An instrument for viewing the inside of the eye, including the retina, optic disc and blood vessels.
The point where the optic nerve leaves the eye. It has no photoreceptors, producing the physiological blind spot.
The nerve that carries visual signals from the retina to the brain.
A very narrow slit beam that shows a thin cross section of the cornea; angled at the limbus it is used to estimate the depth of the peripheral anterior chamber.

source.title: How to Use a Slit Lamp - American Academy of Ophthalmology

definition: The central part of a contact lens that carries the prescription power; its diameter is the optic zone diameter.

source.title: GP Lens Fluorescein Patterns and Troubleshooting

definition: The point on a lens through which light passes without being deviated, so no prism is present. It is normally positioned in front of the pupil.
A noninvasive imaging method that uses light waves to produce cross-sectional images of the retina or anterior eye.
A diagram showing the power in each of a lens’s two principal meridians, used to visualize and calculate sphero-cylindrical powers.

source.title: Optical Cross and Transposition: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: The degree to which a lens converges or diverges light, measured in diopters. Converging (plus) lenses have positive power and diverging (minus) lenses negative power.
A professional who fits, adjusts and dispenses eyeglasses and, where licensed, contact lenses from a prescription written by an optometrist or ophthalmologist.
A doctor of optometry (OD) who examines the eyes, prescribes corrective lenses and diagnoses and treats many eye conditions.
A brand of epoxy resin frame material that becomes very malleable when heated, allowing it to be shaped to the face.

source.title: How to Choose the Glasses Frame Material That's Right for You - American Academy of Ophthalmology

definition: A fitting procedure using specially designed rigid lenses, usually worn overnight, to temporarily reshape the cornea so the wearer sees clearly without lenses during the day.
Oculus sinister, Latin for the left eye (the patient’s left).
The OSHA eye and face protection standard requiring employers to provide suitable protection, compliant with ANSI Z87.1, where workers face eye hazards.

source.title: 1910.133 - Eye and face protection. | Occupational Safety and Health Administration

definition: Oculi uterque, Latin for both eyes.
A refraction performed over a contact lens on the eye to find any power change needed for the final lens.
The total edge-to-edge size of a contact lens. Increasing a soft lens diameter increases its sag and tightens the fit.

source.title: In-Contact Chapter 10: Fitting Soft Contact Lenses (Contamac)

definition: Dk, a material property describing how easily oxygen passes through a lens material (D is the diffusion coefficient and k the solubility). Silicone hydrogels have much higher Dk than conventional hydrogels.
Dk/t, the oxygen permeability of a material divided by the lens thickness, which describes how much oxygen a specific lens delivers to the cornea.

source.title: SILICONE HYDROGELS: FOUR DECADES OF NEW CHEMISTRY IN CONTACT LENSES | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: Pro re nata: as needed.

source.title: List of abbreviations used in medical prescriptions - Wikipedia

definition: An instrument, often ultrasonic or optical, that measures corneal thickness.
Progressive addition lens, a no-line multifocal.

source.title: What Is A Progressive Lens? | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The opening between the upper and lower eyelids; its height and the position of the lids relative to the cornea are recorded before fitting contact lenses.
The tilt of the frame front so the bottom of the lenses is closer to the face than the top. It is usually 5–15°, and each 2° of tilt effectively lowers the optical center about 1 mm.
A moderately narrow slit beam focused on the cornea that shows a three-dimensional block of tissue, used to examine the corneal layers.
Pupillary distance or interpupillary distance: the distance between the pupil centers.
A toric stabilization design (double slab-off) with thin zones at 12 and 6 o’clock and thicker zones at 3 and 9 o’clock; the lids squeeze the thin zones to keep the lens oriented.

source.title: Toric Contact Lens Design: Complete Guide for NCLE Exam

definition: A flatter curve outside the optic zone of a rigid lens that lifts the edge away from the cornea for tear exchange and comfort.

source.title: RGP Contact Lens Fitting: Complete Guide for NCLE Exam

definition: An instrument containing sphere and cylinder lenses, prisms and accessories that the examiner dials in front of the patient’s eyes during a subjective refraction.
A lens that darkens in response to ultraviolet light and fades back indoors. Because car windshields block most UV, many photochromics darken less while driving.

source.title: Photochromic Lenses | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A painful corneal burn from ultraviolet exposure such as welding arcs or snow glare, usually appearing hours after exposure.

source.title: Photokeratitis (ultraviolet [UV] burn, arc eye, snow blindness) - College of Optometrists

definition: Abnormal sensitivity or discomfort in light; disruption of the corneal epithelium, as in keratitis or with a foreign body, is one cause.
Fitting a smaller rigid lens on top of a soft lens to improve rigid lens comfort or centration, often in keratoconus.
A yellowish, raised conjunctival deposit beside the cornea that does not grow onto it; linked to UV exposure and can be irritated by contact lens edges.
An opaque disc with one or more small holes. If acuity improves through the pinhole, the reduced vision is likely due to uncorrected refractive error.
Plano: no refractive power.
Zero refractive power, often written PL or as a sphere of 0.00.
A converging lens, thicker in the center than at the edge, that brings parallel light to a real focus. It corrects hyperopia and presbyopia and acts like two prisms base to base.
A way of writing a sphero-cylindrical prescription with the cylinder as a positive number, traditionally used by many ophthalmologists.
Polymethyl methacrylate, the original hard contact lens plastic. It has essentially no oxygen permeability and has been replaced by gas permeable materials.
The orientation of a light wave’s vibration. Light reflected from flat surfaces such as water or roads is partly horizontally polarized, which is why polarized lenses cut glare.
A lens containing a filter that blocks horizontally polarized light, sharply reducing reflected glare from water, roads and other flat surfaces.

source.title: What Are Polarized Lenses? | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A thermoplastic lens material (index about 1.586, Abbe about 30) that is highly impact resistant and blocks UV inherently. It is the usual choice for children’s, sports and safety eyewear.

source.title: CR-39 vs Poly vs Trivex: Index, Abbe and Weight Chart

definition: Polyhexamethylene biguanide, a large-molecule disinfectant used in many multipurpose solutions.
A family of polymers, such as polyquaternium-1, used as preservatives and disinfectants in multipurpose solutions.
The narrow space between the back of the iris and the front of the crystalline lens and its zonules, filled with aqueous humor.
Adjusting a new frame to the patient (level, pantoscopic tilt, face form, vertex and temple fit) before taking PD and height measurements, so the measurements match how the frame will be worn.
The formula for prism induced by looking away from a lens’s optical center: prism (Δ) = decentration in cm × lens power in diopters (Δ = cF).
The gradual, age-related loss of accommodation that makes near focusing difficult, progressively worsening after about age 40. It is corrected with reading adds, multifocals or monovision.
The process in which a seller sends the prescriber the patient’s lens details; the prescription is passively verified if the prescriber does not respond within eight business hours.

source.title: The Contact Lens Rule: A Guide for Prescribers and Sellers | Federal Trade Commission

definition: A wedge of transparent material with an apex and a base. It bends light toward its base, and the image seen through it appears displaced toward the apex.
A toric stabilization method that adds base-down prism (typically 1.0–1.5Δ) to the lower part of the lens so gravity and the lids keep it oriented.

source.title: Toric Contact Lens Design: Complete Guide for NCLE Exam

definition: The unit of prism power (written Δ). One prism diopter deviates light 1 cm at a distance of 1 m.
The point on a lens where prism is measured. On a progressive it lies midway between the two permanent engravings, which are 34 mm apart.

source.title: Lens Marking Guidelines, Version 2.0 (The Vision Council)

definition: Adding equal vertical prism to both lenses of a progressive to offset the extra thickness at the top of the blank, which results from the steeper lower part of the progressive surface.

source.title: Understanding Prism Thinning | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A lens sold under a store or seller brand. The prescription must name the manufacturer, the private label trade name and any equivalent brand name.

source.title: The Contact Lens Rule: A Guide for Prescribers and Sellers | Federal Trade Commission

definition: A no-line multifocal whose power increases gradually from distance at the top through a corridor to the full near add at the bottom, with unwanted cylinder in the lower side areas.
A Gram-negative bacterium that is a frequent cause of aggressive contact lens–related corneal ulcers.
The condition of having an artificial intraocular lens implanted in place of the natural crystalline lens.
A wedge-shaped growth of conjunctival tissue that extends onto the cornea, usually nasally, linked to UV exposure.
Drooping of the upper eyelid. Long-term rigid contact lens wear is one recognized cause.
The opening in the center of the iris. It constricts in bright light and during near focus and dilates in dim light.
The distance between the centers of the pupils, in millimeters, used to position lens optical centers. It may be measured binocularly or as monocular PDs for each eye.
An instrument that measures binocular and monocular pupillary distance using corneal reflections, at distance and near settings.
Pushing a soft lens upward with the lower lid to judge how easily it moves and how quickly it recenters; the most reliable single test of soft lens tightness.

source.title: Evaluating and Recording Soft Contact Lens Fit (J. Wolffsohn, DOCET)

definition: Quater in die: four times a day.

source.title: List of abbreviations used in medical prescriptions - Wikipedia

definition: The radius of the sphere of which a lens or corneal surface is part. Shorter radii are steeper curves with more power.
Repeated breakdown of the corneal epithelium, often on waking, typically after a previous abrasion or with corneal dystrophy.

source.title: Recurrent corneal epithelial erosion syndrome - College of Optometrists

definition: The percentage of light reflected at a polished lens surface, calculated from the index as ((n−1)/(n+1))². A 1.50 material reflects about 4% per surface, and higher-index materials reflect more.

source.title: How to Choose Lens Material | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The return of light from a surface. For a mirror-like surface the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence; unwanted lens reflections are reduced with anti-reflective coatings.
The bending of light as it passes obliquely from one medium into another with a different index of refraction. It is the principle that gives spectacle and contact lenses their power.
The California registration (RDO) for a business that fills prescriptions for ophthalmic lenses; SLDs and CLDs work within an RDO.

source.title: Frequently Asked Questions – Opticians - California State Board of Optometry

definition: Astigmatism that remains with a spherical contact lens in place, usually lenticular astigmatism or corneal toricity the tear lens cannot correct.
The single combined prism equal to a horizontal and a vertical prism component, found with the Pythagorean theorem; its base direction is given as an angle.

source.title: Resultant Prism Chart | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The light-sensitive inner layer at the back of the eye containing photoreceptors that convert light into nerve signals sent to the brain.
Separation of the retina from the underlying tissue, often heralded by new floaters, flashes or a curtain over vision; it is an emergency.
An inherited retinal degeneration that causes night blindness and progressive loss of peripheral (tunnel) vision.
A handheld instrument that projects a streak or spot of light into the eye so the examiner can judge refractive error from the reflex motion.

An objective technique in which the examiner observes the light reflex in the pupil through trial lenses to measure refractive error. With motion indicates more plus is needed; against motion indicates minus.
Viewing a structure by light reflected from a structure behind it, such as the iris or fundus, so opacities, keratic precipitates and lens vacuoles stand out against the light.
Tilt of the frame front in the opposite direction from pantoscopic, with the lower edge of the lenses farther from the face than the top; it is generally avoided.

source.title: Vertex Distance, Effective Power and Compensated Power (National Academy of Opticianry)

definition: Drops approved for use with contact lenses in the eye to lubricate the lens and relieve dryness.

source.title: How to Take Care of Contact Lenses - American Academy of Ophthalmology

definition: Rigid gas permeable, the class of rigid oxygen-permeable contact lenses.
A rigid contact lens made of oxygen-permeable plastic. It is durable, resists deposits and gives crisp vision, including over corneal astigmatism, but takes longer to adapt to than soft lenses.
Under 21 CFR 886.5916, RGP lenses for daily wear are Class II devices and those for extended wear are Class III.

source.title: eCFR :: 21 CFR 886.5916 -- Rigid gas permeable contact lens.

definition: A frame with no rims, in which lenses are attached by drilling or notching. Polycarbonate or Trivex is recommended because of drilling stress.

source.title: How to Choose the Glasses Frame Material That's Right for You - American Academy of Ophthalmology

definition: Retinal photoreceptors that work in dim light and detect motion but not color; most numerous in the peripheral retina.
A dye used in eye drops or strips to stain damaged conjunctival and corneal cells, helping identify dry eye and other surface disease.
A circular bifocal segment such as the round 22 or 24, with its optical center at the center of the circle. It produces more image jump than a flat-top.

source.title: Bifocal Types & Segment Styles: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: Rubbing lenses with clean fingers and fresh solution, then rinsing, which removes more debris and microbes than soaking alone.

source.title: How to Take Care of Contact Lenses - American Academy of Ophthalmology

definition: Abbreviation for prescription, from the Latin recipe (“take”).

source.title: List of abbreviations used in medical prescriptions - Wikipedia

definition: The depth of a curved surface measured from a chord to the surface. It underlies lens thickness calculations and the sagittal depth of contact lenses.
The height of a lens’s back surface over a given chord. Fit is governed by sag: steepening the base curve or enlarging the diameter increases sag and tightens the fit.

source.title: RULES OF THUMB | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: Sterile salt solution used to rinse lenses after cleaning and before insertion. It does not disinfect.

The rigid lens power rule “Steeper Add Minus, Flatter Add Plus”: when the base curve is changed, compensate the lens power for the change in tear lens power (about 0.25 D per 0.05 mm near typical K values).
aliases: steeper add minus flatter add plus

definition: A test of tear production that measures how far tears wet a small paper strip placed at the lower lid margin over five minutes.
The tough, white, opaque outer coat of the eyeball that protects it and maintains its shape.
A large-diameter rigid gas permeable lens that vaults the cornea and rests on the sclera, holding a fluid reservoir over the cornea. It is used for irregular corneas and severe dry eye.
Painful inflammation of the sclera, often associated with systemic inflammatory disease.
Directing a narrow beam at the limbus so light travels through the cornea by internal reflection, creating a glowing ring around the cornea that highlights corneal pathology.
A hard coat applied to plastic lenses to make the surface more resistant to scratching. It does not make a lens scratch-proof.

source.title: What is an AR (Anti-Reflective) Coating? | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Inadequate edge clearance that blocks tear exchange under a rigid lens and can cause the lens to adhere to the cornea.
The vertical distance from the lowest point of the lens opening (where it sits in the frame) up to the top of the bifocal segment line.

source.title: Bifocal Types & Segment Styles: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: A lens blank with a finished front curve whose back surface is ground and polished by the lab to produce the prescription.

source.title: All About Lens Surfacing | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Common shorthand for silicone hydrogel lens materials.

source.title: SILICONE HYDROGELS: FOUR DECADES OF NEW CHEMISTRY IN CONTACT LENSES | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: A soft lens material combining silicone, which carries oxygen, with hydrogel components. It gives much higher Dk than conventional hydrogels and made safe overnight wear practical.

source.title: SILICONE HYDROGELS: FOUR DECADES OF NEW CHEMISTRY IN CONTACT LENSES | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: A multifocal contact lens that presents distance and near powers to the eye at the same time, with center-distance, center-near or aspheric optics; the brain selects the clearer image.

source.title: FINE-TUNE YOUR MULTIFOCAL LENS FITTING | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: A lens with one prescription power throughout, used for distance, intermediate or near only.

source.title: Basic Lens Styles and Types | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: An autoimmune disease that attacks moisture-producing glands, causing severe dry eye and dry mouth; it can make contact lens wear difficult.
A lens surfacing technique (bicentric grinding) that removes base-up prism from the lower part of the more minus (or less plus) lens to reduce vertical imbalance at near.

source.title: What Is A Slab-Off Lens? | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A biomicroscope combining a high-intensity adjustable light source with a binocular microscope, used to examine the eye and evaluate contact lens fit.
The law relating the angles of incidence and refraction: n1 sin i = n2 sin r. Light bends toward the normal when it enters a denser (higher-index) medium and away from it when it leaves.
The standard eye chart of letters of decreasing size used to measure visual acuity, recorded as a fraction such as 20/20.
A flexible lens made of water-containing plastic (hydrogel or silicone hydrogel) that drapes over the cornea and extends past the limbus. It is usually comfortable right away.
A material’s density compared with water. A lower specific gravity means a lighter lens of the same size and power.

source.title: How to Choose Lens Material | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Blurred vision with glasses after removing contact lenses, a sign of corneal edema or reshaping (warpage).

source.title: GP Fit: Steep vs. Flat - Characteristics, Consequences, and Correction

definition: California’s individual registration (SLD) to fit and adjust spectacle lenses without direct supervision. Applicants must pass the ABO exam and work in a registered dispensing business.

source.title: ABO-NCLE - California State Board of Optometry

definition: A slit lamp technique in which the angle of illumination equals the angle of observation, creating a bright reflex used to judge the smoothness of the corneal and lens surfaces and to view the endothelial mosaic.
The spherical component of a prescription, giving equal power in all meridians, in diopters (plus for hyperopia, minus for myopia).
A lens error in which peripheral rays focus at a different point than paraxial rays. Aspheric designs reduce it.
The sphere plus half the cylinder. It is the single sphere power that places the circle of least confusion on the retina, often used to choose a spherical soft lens.
Making a soft lens by spinning liquid polymer in a rotating mold so centripetal force shapes the back surface.
A hinge with a built-in spring that lets the temple flex outward, improving durability and fit.
A nickel-free, hypoallergenic frame metal that holds its shape well.
Depth perception that comes from the brain combining the slightly different images seen by the two eyes.
A misalignment of the eyes so they do not point at the same object; may be constant or intermittent.
A bright red patch from a broken blood vessel under the conjunctiva; it looks alarming but is usually harmless.

An arc-shaped epithelial split in the superior cornea within about 2 mm of the limbus, caused mechanically by soft lenses, especially stiff silicone hydrogels. Wear stops until it heals, then a different material or design is tried.

source.title: Contact Lens-related Complications: A Review (J Ophthalmic Vis Res, PMC)

definition: Inflammation and staining of the superior bulbar conjunctiva, limbus and cornea. The contact lens–induced form has historically been strongly linked to thimerosal-containing solutions; switching to preservative-free care and fresh lenses helps.

source.title: Contact Lens-induced Superior Limbic | Contact Lens Spectrum

definition: The lab process of generating and polishing a lens’s back surface to create the prescribed power, cylinder and prism.

source.title: All About Lens Surfacing | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A detergent-like compound that loosens debris and oils from a lens surface; it is the active ingredient in daily cleaners.
Single vision: a lens with one power throughout.

source.title: Basic Lens Styles and Types | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Ter in die: three times a day.

source.title: List of abbreviations used in medical prescriptions - Wikipedia

definition: A medium-wide beam with the illumination arm swung about 90° from the microscope, giving an oblique view of the cornea, the undilated iris and the anterior lens surface.
The time, in seconds, between a blink and the first dry spot in the fluorescein-stained tear film. A short TBUT indicates an unstable tear film and higher risk of lens intolerance.
The thin layer of tears covering the cornea and conjunctiva. It is classically described as three layers: an outer lipid layer, a middle aqueous layer and an inner mucin layer.
The lens of tears trapped between a rigid lens and the cornea. A lens steeper than K creates a plus tear lens; flatter than K creates a minus tear lens.
An optical system that magnifies distant objects; small spectacle-mounted or handheld telescopes are used as low-vision aids.
The arm of a frame that runs from the hinge over the ear. Its length and bend affect how securely the frame holds its fit.
A plastic that softens when heated and can be re-molded, such as polycarbonate. Thermoset materials such as CR-39 cure permanently and do not re-soften.

source.title: CR-39 vs Poly vs Trivex: Index, Abbe and Weight Chart

definition: A mercury-based preservative once common in lens solutions and a frequent cause of solution sensitivity reactions.
A lens whose thickness is small relative to its radii, so power can be approximated as the simple sum of its surface powers.
A color added to a lens to reduce light transmission, improve contrast for specific tasks such as sports or driving, or for fashion.

source.title: Lens Coatings & Treatments: Enhancing Vision and Function | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A frame made of 90–100% titanium: extremely light, strong, corrosion resistant and hypoallergenic, though rimless titanium needs the right tools to adjust.
An instrument that measures intraocular pressure, an important screening test for glaucoma.
An eye drop that numbs the cornea; some practitioners use it during an initial rigid lens fitting to ease adaptation.
A lens with different powers in two perpendicular meridians, used to correct astigmatism in spectacles and contact lenses.
Complete reflection of light back into a denser medium when it strikes the boundary at more than the critical angle. It is why light cannot exit some surfaces and is used in prisms and fiber optics.
Diffuse redness, stinging and corneal staining caused by sensitivity to preservatives in lens care solutions, historically thimerosal.
Coaxial illumination through the pupil so defects in the iris show up as light passing through tissue.
Converting a prescription between plus- and minus-cylinder form: add the cylinder to the sphere, change the cylinder’s sign, and change the axis by 90°.

source.title: Transposing Prescriptions | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: A lens with three powers: distance, an intermediate segment and a near segment, each separated by a line.

A lens material introduced by PPG in 2001 (index 1.53, specific gravity 1.11, the lightest available) that combines impact resistance comparable to polycarbonate with better optics and the tensile strength drill mounts need.

source.title: How to Choose Lens Material | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: Cutting a flat edge, usually at the bottom, of a lens so the lower lid holds it in orientation; it can be less comfortable.

source.title: Toric Contact Lens Design: Complete Guide for NCLE Exam

definition: A hydrogen peroxide system in which neutralization is a separate step, such as rinsing with saline or adding a tablet after disinfection.
A one-piece bifocal with a very large round segment; the Ultex A is 38 mm across with its optical center 19 mm below the segment top.

source.title: Bifocal Types & Segment Styles: Complete Guide for ABO Exam

definition: Invisible radiation with wavelengths shorter than visible violet light (below about 400 nm). It is divided into UVA, UVB and UVC bands, and long-term exposure can harm the eyes.

A label meaning a lens absorbs ultraviolet light up to 400 nm. CR-39 lenses are commonly dyed with a UV-absorbing treatment, and Laramy-K cautions that some treatments fall short of 400 nm, so verify with a meter that reads at 400 nm.

source.title: The Problem with UV 400 Treatments | Laramy-K Independent Optical Lab

definition: The middle, vascular layer of the eye made up of the iris, ciliary body and choroid.
Inflammation of the uvea. Anterior uveitis (iritis) causes pain, light sensitivity and redness around the cornea and requires medical care.
Visual acuity, the sharpness of vision.
A raised, inflamed, vascularized lesion at the peripheral cornea and limbus, usually in long-term GP wearers; large or steep lenses and low edge lift are thought to trigger it.
The amount of convergence or divergence of light at a given point, expressed in diopters as the reciprocal of the distance (in meters) to the point of focus.
The distance between the back surface of a spectacle lens and the front of the cornea. It matters for powers above about ±4.00 D because changing it changes the effective power.
A difference in vertical prism between the two eyes when looking through points below or above the optical centers, common in anisometropia at the reading level. It may be corrected with slab-off.
A highly contagious conjunctival infection, often adenoviral, causing redness, watery discharge and sometimes a preceding cold.
The portion of the electromagnetic spectrum the eye can see, roughly 380 to 750 nm, from violet (short) to red (long).
The clarity or sharpness of vision, usually measured with a letter chart and written as a Snellen fraction (e.g., 20/40).
A test that maps the extent of peripheral and central vision, used to detect field loss from glaucoma and neurological disease.
The clear gel that fills the large space between the lens and the retina.
The percentage of a hydrated soft lens’s weight that is water. In the FDA scheme, low water is under 50% and high water 50% or more.

source.title: List of soft contact lens materials - Wikipedia

definition: The distance between successive peaks of a wave. In optics it is usually given in nanometers, and it determines the color of visible light.
How readily tears spread over a lens surface. It is measured by the wetting (contact) angle; a lower angle means better wetting.
Astigmatism in which the vertical corneal meridian is steepest; corrected with minus cylinder near axis 180.
A test of binocular fusion using red-green glasses and a light with four dots; the number of dots seen indicates fusion, suppression or diplopia.
A yellow barrier filter placed over the slit lamp’s observation system to enhance the contrast of fluorescein patterns.
Yellowish cholesterol deposits on or around the eyelids.
Fine fibers that suspend the crystalline lens from the ciliary body and transmit changes in ciliary muscle tension to the lens.
Cellulose acetate, the most common plastic frame material, cut from sheet stock. It is adjusted with heat (about 120 °C per the 20/20 guide), and acetone dissolves it.
